title: Passenger Terminal at Riyadh Airport Hit Again, Just One Day After 12 Fatalities — AP News
body:
A second projectile slammed into the passenger terminal of Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, just 24 hours after a missile strike on the same complex killed 12 people and forced the airport’s closure. Saudi officials confirmed the new impact caused no additional casualties, but the repeated attacks have heightened regional tensions and raised fresh questions about the security of the kingdom’s critical infrastructure.

The latest strike hit the terminal’s western wing, where the earlier missile had ripped through the roof and ignited a fire that claimed the lives of airport workers and passengers. Emergency crews quickly extinguished the blaze and secured the area, but the damage was enough to keep the airport shut indefinitely. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Interior said the projectile was intercepted by air‑defence systems before it could reach the building’s core, limiting the physical harm. Nonetheless, the incident underscores the vulnerability of one of the Gulf’s busiest aviation hubs, which handles more than 30 million passengers annually.

The attacks are being attributed to the Houthi movement in Yemen, a Iran‑aligned rebel group that has escalated its missile and drone campaign against Saudi targets since the war in Yemen intensified in 2015. The Houthis have previously claimed responsibility for strikes on oil facilities, shipping lanes and other strategic sites across the Red Sea and Arabian Peninsula. While they have not officially confirmed responsibility for the Riyadh airport attacks, their pattern of targeting high‑profile civilian and economic assets aligns with the recent assaults. Saudi Arabia’s coalition forces, which include the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and other Gulf states, have responded with air raids on Houthi positions in northern Yemen, further inflaming the already volatile conflict.

The repercussions of the airport shutdown extend beyond immediate travel disruptions. King Khalid International serves as a gateway for both business travelers and pilgrims heading to the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, especially during the Hajj season. Airlines have rerouted flights to secondary airports such as Riyadh’s Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz Airport and the neighboring King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah, leading to congestion, higher ticket prices and logistical challenges for cargo shipments. The Saudi aviation sector, which contributes billions of riyals to the national economy, now faces a test of resilience as it seeks alternative routes and reinforces security protocols.

Analysts note that the attacks could signal a broader strategic shift by the Houthis, who appear to be expanding their operational reach deeper into Saudi territory. “Hitting a major international airport is a symbolic move designed to demonstrate capability and to pressure the Saudi leadership,” said Dr. Laila Al‑Mansour, a regional security expert at the Gulf Research Center. “It forces the kingdom to divert resources to air defence and crisis management, potentially weakening its focus on the Yemen front.” The incident also raises concerns about the effectiveness of Saudi Arabia’s layered missile‑defence architecture, which includes U.S.-supplied Patriot batteries and domestically produced systems.

International reactions have been swift. The United States condemned the attacks, calling them “unacceptable acts of aggression” and reiterating its commitment to Saudi security under existing defense agreements. The European Union urged all parties to de‑escalate and protect civilian infrastructure, while the United Nations called for an immediate cease‑fire in Yemen to prevent further spillover into neighboring states.

As Saudi authorities assess the damage and plan a phased reopening of King Khalid International, the broader geopolitical landscape remains uncertain. The kingdom is likely to bolster its air‑defence posture, possibly accelerating procurement of advanced interceptors and enhancing coordination with allied forces. Meanwhile, the Houthis may seek to leverage the heightened attention to extract political concessions or to press their demands in ongoing diplomatic talks. The coming weeks will reveal whether Riyadh can restore full airport operations and whether the recent assaults will trigger a wider escalation in the already fraught Middle‑East security environment.
